opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in layers. Openness isn't all-or-nothing; it's about what creates the most value for the ecosystem and what keeps us able to keep pushing the frontier.

At the model level, we've become fairly open. Releasing weights and sharing technical reports does a few things for us. It lets developers and partner companies build on our work without being locked in. It earns trust, because people can see what the model actually does. And it creates a feedback loop: the community finds problems, builds tooling, and adapts the model to scenarios we would never have covered ourselves. For a company our size, that leverage is very important. You can't do everything yourself.

But open-sourcing a model isn't the same as giving away everything. What really determines your long-term position isn't one checkpoint. It's the capability to keep producing better ones: the data pipelines, the training infrastructure, the methods for scaling reinforcement learning, and the team's accumulated intuition about what works. Those are harder to transfer, and they matter more. So when we work with other companies, we're quite willing to share the model, the interfaces, and even a lot of methodology through papers. The deeper engineering know-how is something we keep investing in internally.

There's also a mindset point. In this field, any single technical advantage has a short half-life. If you protect something too tightly, it may be obsolete in six months anyway. So I'd rather compete on speed of iteration than on secrecy. If openness helps more people use our models, gives us more real-world signal, and pushes the whole field forward, then the cost of sharing is usually smaller than people imagine.

With partners specifically, the principle is mutual value. They bring scenarios, distribution, or domain data we don't have. We bring model capability and support for adapting it. The question is never "how little can we give?" but "what combination lets both sides grow?" If the cooperation only works because one side is hiding things, it probably won't last.

So my short answer: be generous with what helps the ecosystem, and focus your own energy on the thing that can't easily be copied, which is the ability to keep getting better.

r001.rationale: The response says open-sourcing a model is not the same as giving away everything, and says deeper engineering know-how stays internal when working with partners.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think of open-sourcing as a question of where the value actually sits, rather than an ideological stance. For us at Moonshot, the core is the model, the training recipe, and the data pipeline. Those are things you accumulate over years, and they compound. So when we cooperate with other companies, we're very open about the layers that help the ecosystem grow around our models, things like inference frameworks, tooling, evaluation methods, even some of the research findings, because that creates more scenarios where the model gets used, and more usage comes back to us as signal.

But I also don't think "closed is safer" is automatically true. In this field, if you don't share anything, you fall out of the conversation, and talent and partners stop coming to you. So the question I ask is: does releasing this help the model improve faster through the community, or does it just hand the result to someone who can copy it without bearing the cost? If it's the former, we release it, and sometimes even things that feel uncomfortable to release. If it's the latter, we hold.

The other thing I'd say is that the real moat today isn't the weights of a single model. A model is a snapshot. The moat is the ability to produce the next one, and the one after that, faster than others. If you believe in that, you can be fairly generous with the snapshots and still protect the engine. That's roughly the balance we try to strike: give partners enough to build real products and trust us, keep the parts that make the next generation possible.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes selectively sharing ecosystem layers while holding back the core model-building capabilities, making clear that collaboration need not mean open-sourcing all technology.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is what we want to achieve through the cooperation. If the goal is to help more people build on the technology, then open-sourcing can be very valuable. It lowers the cost of adoption and gives partners more confidence that they can control what they’re building.

But cooperation doesn’t necessarily mean opening everything. I would distinguish between what needs to be shared for the collaboration to work and what represents each company’s core advantage. You can share interfaces, tools, or particular components while keeping other parts proprietary.

The important thing is to make those boundaries clear early: what each side contributes, what can be released, and how jointly developed work will be used. I’d think about it less as a percentage of technology to open-source and more as whether the arrangement gives both sides a reason to keep investing.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperation does not mean opening everything and that some parts can remain proprietary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to be clear about what you want to achieve through cooperation. If the goal is to help more developers adopt a technology and build an ecosystem around it, open-sourcing can be very valuable. But cooperation doesn’t necessarily mean opening up everything. You can share interfaces, tools, or particular components while keeping other parts proprietary.

For me, the important question is whether the arrangement creates value for both sides and gives both sides an incentive to keep investing. I wouldn’t decide based on a fixed percentage of technology to open-source. I’d look at what needs to be shared to make the collaboration work, and where our core differentiation lies.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperation does not necessarily mean opening up everything and that some parts can remain proprietary.
